handsOnLab.brief: Implement the module's number theory from scratch in Python — Euclid, extended Euclid, modular inverse, RSA keygen/encrypt/decrypt, and Diffie-Hellman — using only integer arithmetic, and verify every hand calculation from the notes.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Script prints gcd(1071,462)=21, inverse 2753 (verified by multiplication), RSA round trip 65→2790→65, DH shared secret 2 computed both ways — all matching the notes exactly.
handsOnLab.deliverable: numtheory-lab.py (euclid, egcd, modinv, rsa_keygen/encrypt/decrypt, diffie_hellman) + lab-notes.md (hand-vs-machine table, one paragraph on why toy sizes don't transfer to production).
steps: Create ~/il29-m30-lab/numtheory-lab.py. Implement euclid(a,b) returning (gcd, steps_list) with each (a,b,q,r) recorded.
Assert euclid(1071,462)[0]==21 and print the steps; compare to the notes.
Implement egcd(a,b) returning (g,x,y) with ax+by=g. Implement modinv(a,n)=x% n; assert modinv(17,3120)==2753.
Implement rsa_keygen(p,q,e): return dict(n=p*q, phi=(p-1)*(q-1), e=e, d=modinv(e,phi)). Run with (61,53,17); assert n==3233, phi==3120, d==2753.
Implement rsa_encrypt(m,pub) and rsa_decrypt(c,priv) with pow(m,e,n). Round-trip m=65: assert encrypt→2790 and decrypt→65.

Run the script fresh; every assert passes.

notes.body:
Cryptography is number theory with consequences, so we build from the ground up. Divisibility: a divides b (written a | b) if b = a·k for some integer k. 7 | 42 because 42 = 7×6; 7 ∤ 43. A prime is a natural number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, ... Note that 1 is not prime (it would break unique factorization) and 2 is the only even prime. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every integer greater than 1 factors uniquely into primes. Worked factorization: 2024. It is even: 2024 = 2 × 1012 = 2² × 506 = 2³ × 253. Now 253: test divisibility — not even, 2+5+3=10 so not divisible by 3, doesn't end in 5, 7×36=252 so 253 = 7×36+1, not divisible by 7. Try 11: 11×23 = 253. Yes. So 2024 = 2³ × 11 × 23. Check: 8×11=88, 88×23=2024 ✓. This mechanical process — trial division — is how factoring works conceptually, and its slowness on large numbers is literally what RSA's security rests on: multiplying primes is easy, un-multiplying (factoring) is hard. The greatest common divisor, gcd(a,b), is the largest integer dividing both. gcd(12,18)=6. Two numbers with gcd 1 are coprime (relatively prime) — 8 and 15 are coprime, 8 and 12 are not. Coprimality is the gatekeeper concept of this module: RSA needs e coprime to φ(n), Euler's theorem needs a coprime to n, inverses exist only for coprime pairs. Worked: are 17 and 3120 coprime? You could factor both, but Euclid (next note) answers in three divisions. Common mistake: calling 1 prime, or assuming 'odd' means 'prime' — 9, 15, 21, 25 are all odd composites. Test, don't assume.

Trial division works for 2024 and dies for 600-digit numbers — so how does anyone find RSA primes? Probabilistic primality tests: Miller-Rabin and friends do not prove primality, they bound the error — each round roughly halves the chance the number is composite, so forty rounds give an error probability around 2 to the minus 80, smaller than the chance of a cosmic ray flipping your answer. The operational point: 'prime' in production means 'passed enough Miller-Rabin rounds with good randomness,' and the randomness matters as much as the test — a predictable 'random' candidate generator produces predictable primes. Also note the prime number theorem's practical gift: among 600-digit numbers, roughly 1 in 1,384 is prime, so generating a prime means testing about 1,384 candidates — each test fast, the pipeline parallelizable. Key generation takes seconds, not eons, because primes are dense enough and tests are cheap. The asymmetry RSA needs (multiply easy, factor hard) survives: finding primes is easy, factoring their product is not. Do not implement your own primality test for production — use the vetted library — but understand what it guarantees, because 'probably prime' with a quantified error bound is the actual foundation your keys stand on.
notes.title: Divisibility, primes, and factorization

notes.body:
The gcd is everywhere in crypto, and Euclid's algorithm computes it without factoring — which matters because factoring is the hard problem. The algorithm: to find gcd(a,b), divide a by b, keep the remainder r; then repeat with (b, r); when a remainder hits 0, the last nonzero remainder is the gcd. Why it works: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b), because any common divisor of a and b also divides the remainder, and vice versa — the set of common divisors doesn't change, only the numbers shrink. Worked — the full computation of gcd(1071, 462). Step 1: 1071 ÷ 462 = 2 remainder 147 (2×462 = 924; 1071−924 = 147). Step 2: 462 ÷ 147 = 3 remainder 21 (3×147 = 441; 462−441 = 21). Step 3: 147 ÷ 21 = 7 remainder 0 (7×21 = 147 exactly). Remainder 0 — stop. Last nonzero remainder: 21. So gcd(1071,462) = 21. Three divisions replaced factoring two four-digit numbers. The algorithm is fast because remainders shrink geometrically — the number of steps is logarithmic, which is why it scales to thousand-digit numbers while trial division doesn't. The extended Euclidean algorithm goes one step further: it finds integers x, y with ax + by = gcd(a,b) (Bézout's identity). When gcd(a,n)=1, this gives ax + ny = 1, so ax ≡ 1 (mod n) — x is the modular inverse of a. Worked — inverse of 17 mod 3120 (you need this for RSA next). Forward: 3120 = 183×17 + 9 (183×17=3111). 17 = 1×9 + 8. 9 = 1×8 + 1. 8 = 8×1 + 0. Now unwind: 1 = 9 − 1×8 = 9 − (17 − 9) = 2×9 − 17 = 2×(3120 − 183×17) − 17 = 2×3120 − 366×17 − 17 = 2×3120 − 367×17. So (−367)×17 ≡ 1 (mod 3120); reduce −367 mod 3120: −367 + 3120 = 2753. The inverse is 2753. Verify: 17×2753 = 46801 = 15×3120 + 1 ✓. Common mistake: assuming inverses always exist — 6 has no inverse mod 10 (gcd(6,10)=2≠1). Inverse exists iff coprime.

Euclid's algorithm appears in more places than key generation. RSA keygen uses it twice: verifying gcd(e, phi(n)) = 1 when choosing e, and the extended version computing d. Diffie-Hellman parameter validation checks gcd relationships. But the most operational appearance is in the Chinese Remainder Theorem computations inside fast RSA implementations (CRT decryption, which splits the work mod p and mod q — the reason RSA decryption is faster than the naive exponentiation suggests). There is also a lovely efficiency fact worth internalizing: Euclid's algorithm on consecutive Fibonacci numbers is the worst case, and even then it is logarithmic — Lame's theorem bounds the steps at five times the digit count. For thousand-digit numbers that is a few thousand divisions: trivial. Contrast with factoring the same numbers: infeasible. This is the recurring theme of the module — the easy-versus-hard asymmetry between gcd and factoring is load-bearing for all of public-key crypto. When someone proposes a 'new' cryptosystem, the first question is always: where is the asymmetry, and does it survive the known algorithms? Euclid is the easy side; make sure the hard side is actually hard.
notes.title: Euclid's algorithm and the extended version

notes.body:
Modular arithmetic is arithmetic on remainders — clock arithmetic, and the native language of crypto. a ≡ b (mod n) ('a is congruent to b mod n') means n divides (a−b): same remainder upon division by n. 17 ≡ 5 (mod 12) — 17:00 is 5 PM. −3 ≡ 9 (mod 12). The congruence classes mod n are the n possible remainders {0, 1, ..., n−1}, and every integer lives in exactly one class. The miracle that makes it all work: you can reduce mod n at any point during + and ×. (a+b) mod n = ((a mod n) + (b mod n)) mod n; same for multiplication. Worked: (7+15) mod 12: 7+15=22, 22 mod 12 = 10. Via reduction: (7+15) mod 12 = 10 ✓. (7×15) mod 12: 7×15=105; 105 = 8×12+9, so 9. Via reduction first: 7×15 mod 12 = (7 mod 12)×(15 mod 12) = 7×3 = 21, 21 mod 12 = 9 ✓. Same answer, smaller numbers — and for thousand-digit numbers this is the difference between possible and impossible. Exponentiation mod n never computes the giant power: 5^6 mod 23 via square-and-multiply: 5²=25≡2 (mod 23); 5⁴≡2²=4; 5⁶=5⁴×5²≡4×2=8 (mod 23). Every intermediate stayed below 23²=529. This is how RSA and Diffie-Hellman actually compute — pow(base, exp, mod) in Python does exactly this. Division mod n means multiplication by the inverse (previous note): 1/17 mod 3120 is 2753, i.e., x/17 ≡ 2753x (mod 3120). Worked mini-equation: solve 3x ≡ 7 (mod 10). Inverse of 3 mod 10: 3×7=21≡1, so inverse is 7. x ≡ 7×7 = 49 ≡ 9 (mod 10). Check: 3×9=27≡7 ✓. Common mistake: 'cancelling' across a modulus like ordinary division — 6x ≡ 6 (mod 10) does not imply x ≡ 1 (mod 10) (x=6 works too: 36≡6). Division mod n is only safe via the inverse, which only exists for coprime denominators.

One more production reality that the clock arithmetic hides: timing. Square-and-multiply as naively implemented takes different amounts of time depending on the exponent's bits (it multiplies only when the bit is 1) — and that timing leaks the private exponent to anyone who can measure operation times. This is a side-channel attack: the math is correct and the implementation betrays it. Production modular exponentiation is constant-time — every bit costs the same operations — and often uses Montgomery representation to make the modular reductions themselves uniform. The lesson generalizes: in crypto, the algorithm and its physical execution are different things, and attackers live in the gap. When you evaluate crypto implementations (rather than the math), ask about constant-time guarantees, blinding (randomizing the computation per run), and cache behavior. The number theory in this module tells you whether the scheme is sound; the implementation discipline tells you whether the deployment is. Both have failed in the real world — and the math being right never saved a leaky implementation.
notes.title: Modular arithmetic: the clockwork of crypto

notes.body:
Euler's theorem is the engine inside RSA — understand it and RSA stops being magic. First, the totient: φ(n) counts the integers from 1 to n that are coprime to n. For a prime p, every smaller positive integer is coprime to p, so φ(p) = p−1. For n = pq with distinct primes, φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1) — count: n − p − q + 1 = (p−1)(q−1). Check with n=10: numbers coprime to 10 are 1,3,7,9 — φ(10)=4 ✓. Euler's theorem: if gcd(a,n)=1, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). Worked verification with a=3, n=10: φ(10)=4; 3⁴=81; 81 mod 10 = 1 ✓. Another: a=2, n=7 (φ(7)=6): 2⁶=64; 64 = 9×7+1, so 64≡1 (mod 7) ✓. Why it's true, intuitively: multiplying the φ(n) coprime residues by a just permutes them (a is invertible mod n, so no two collide and none leaves the set); the product of the set therefore equals a^φ(n) times itself, and cancelling the product (legal — it's coprime to n) leaves a^φ(n) ≡ 1. Fermat's little theorem is the prime case: a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for a not divisible by p — Euler with φ(p)=p−1. Why RSA needs it: RSA decryption computes (m^e)^d = m^(ed), and key generation arranges ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)), i.e., ed = kφ(n)+1. Then m^(ed) = m^(kφ+1) = (m^φ)^k × m ≡ 1^k × m = m (mod n) — Euler's theorem applied k times, for m coprime to n. (The full proof handles m sharing a factor with n via the Chinese Remainder Theorem; the mechanism is the same.) So Euler's theorem is not background — it is the correctness proof of RSA, and you are about to watch it work on real numbers. Common mistake: applying Euler when a and n aren't coprime — the theorem's hypothesis matters; RSA keygen's choice of e coprime to φ(n) is load-bearing, not decorative.

A refinement worth knowing exists: the Carmichael function lambda(n), the smallest exponent with a to the lambda congruent to 1 for all a coprime to n. Euler's theorem uses phi(n), which always works but is not always minimal — lambda(n) divides phi(n) and is sometimes much smaller. For n = pq, lambda(n) = lcm(p-1, q-1). In our RSA example: lcm(60, 52) = 780 (60 = 4x3x5, 52 = 4x13, lcm = 4x3x5x13 = 780). So actually a^780 is congruent to 1 mod 3233 for all coprime a — decryption needs only ed congruent to 1 mod 780, not mod 3120. Check: 46801 mod 780 = 46801 - 60x780 = 46801 - 46800 = 1. Real RSA implementations use lambda(n) (via CRT) for the private exponent computation because smaller exponents mean faster decryption. You do not need Carmichael for the exam-style understanding — Euler's phi version is the correct, provable foundation — but when you read library code and see lcm(p-1, q-1), you will know what it is: the tightest version of the theorem you just learned. The pattern is general: learn the clean theorem first (Euler), then the optimized refinement (Carmichael) as 'the same idea, sharpened.' Mathematics rewards this two-pass approach everywhere.
notes.title: Euler's theorem: the engine inside RSA

notes.body:
Now the full RSA construction with small primes, every number verified. Key generation. Pick two distinct primes: p=61, q=53. Compute n = p×q = 61×53 = 3233. Compute φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1) = 60×52 = 3120. Choose e coprime to 3120 with 1<e<3120: e=17 (gcd(17,3120)=1 ✓ — 3120=183×17+9, and Euclid confirms). Compute d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n) = 17⁻¹ mod 3120 = 2753 (extended Euclid, previous note; verified: 17×2753=46801=15×3120+1). Public key: (n=3233, e=17). Private key: (n=3233, d=2753). Encryption. Message m=65 (must be < n). c = m^e mod n = 65^17 mod 3233. Via square-and-multiply (never compute 65^17 directly — it has 30 digits): c = 2790. Decryption. m = c^d mod n = 2790^2753 mod 3233 = 65. Round trip: 65 → 2790 → 65 ✓. Why decryption works — the exponent arithmetic: ed = 17×2753 = 46801. Divide by φ(n)=3120: 46801 = 15×3120 + 1 (15×3120=46800). So (m^e)^d = m^46801 = m^(15×3120+1) = (m^3120)^15 × m ≡ 1^15 × m = m (mod 3233), by Euler's theorem (φ(3233)=3120). The eavesdropper sees n=3233, e=17, c=2790 — recovering m requires d, which requires φ(n), which requires factoring 3233. Factoring 3233 is trivial (it's 61×53); factoring a 600-digit n is not — that asymmetry is the entire security of RSA. Signing uses the same math reversed: sign with the private key (s = m^d mod n), verify with the public key (m = s^e mod n) — only the private-key holder could have produced s. Common mistake: thinking small-prime RSA is 'broken RSA' — the mechanism is exactly right; only the sizes are toys. Real deployments use primes hundreds of digits long and careful padding; the number theory you just did is identical.

Textbook RSA has a sharp edge worth seeing once: it is malleable. Given c = m^e, an attacker computes (2^e times c) mod n = (2m)^e mod n — a valid encryption of 2m, without knowing m. And it is deterministic: same m, same c, every time — so attackers can test guesses ('is this ciphertext the encryption of YES?'). These are not theoretical: chosen-ciphertext attacks exploit malleability to decrypt messages by asking the victim to decrypt crafted ciphertexts. The fix is padding — OAEP for encryption, PSS for signatures — which randomizes the plaintext before exponentiation and adds verifiable structure, killing both determinism and malleability. This is why the module keeps saying 'never deploy textbook RSA': the number theory is right and the scheme is broken without padding. When you audit a system using RSA, the questions are: which padding, is it verified on decryption (not just applied on encryption), and are decryption failures handled without oracles (no 'padding invalid' versus 'decryption failed' timing or behavior differences — that is the padding-oracle attack). The math you verified is the engine; padding is the chassis. An engine without a chassis does not get you anywhere safely.
notes.title: RSA end-to-end with small primes

notes.body:
Diffie-Hellman lets two parties agree on a secret over a public channel — no prior shared secret, eavesdroppers see everything except the secret itself. Public parameters: a prime p and a generator g. Alice picks secret a, sends A = g^a mod p. Bob picks secret b, sends B = g^b mod p. Alice computes S = B^a mod p; Bob computes S = A^b mod p. Both get g^(ab) mod p — the same value — while the eavesdropper, who saw p, g, A, B, faces the discrete logarithm problem: recovering a from g^a mod p. Worked with small numbers — every value verified. p=23, g=5. Alice's secret: a=6. A = 5^6 mod 23: 5²=25≡2; 5⁴≡2²=4; 5⁶=5⁴×5²≡4×2=8 (mod 23). Alice sends 8. Bob's secret: b=15. B = 5^15 mod 23 = 19 (via square-and-multiply: 5⁸≡4²=16, 5^15=5⁸×5⁴×5²×5¹≡16×4×2×5=640; 640 mod 23: 23×27=621, 640−621=19 ✓). Bob sends 19. Alice computes S = B^a = 19^6 mod 23: 19≡−4; (−4)²=16; (−4)⁴=256≡256−253=3 (23×11=253); (−4)^6=(−4)⁴×(−4)²≡3×16=48≡48−46=2 (mod 23). S=2. Bob computes S = A^b = 8^15 mod 23: 8²=64≡64−46=18; 8⁴≡18²=324≡324−322=2 (23×14=322); 8⁸≡2²=4; 8^15=8⁸×8⁴×8²×8≡4×2×18×8=1152; 1152 mod 23: 23×50=1150, remainder 2 ✓. S=2. Both sides agree: 2. The eavesdropper saw p=23, g=5, A=8, B=19 — and nothing else. To find the secret they'd solve 5^a≡8 (mod 23), trivial here (a=6 by trying), infeasible for 2000-bit p. This is the ancestor of every TLS handshake's key agreement: the modern versions use elliptic curves, but the idea — public values, private exponents, shared secret from exponent arithmetic — is Diffie-Hellman 1976, unchanged. Common mistake: thinking the shared secret can be sent instead of computed — it never crosses the wire. The wire carries only the public values; the secret exists solely as matching computations at both ends.

Two things the basic exchange lacks, both operationally critical. First, authentication: Diffie-Hellman alone is anonymous — nothing stops an attacker from sitting in the middle, doing one exchange with Alice and another with Bob, and relaying messages while reading everything. The math is perfect and the protocol is trivially man-in-the-middled. Real deployments authenticate the exchange: sign the public values (TLS certificates), or use pre-shared keys or password-based variants. Never deploy unauthenticated DH — the eavesdropper model in the drill assumed passive observation; the active attacker breaks it completely. Second, forward secrecy: if Alice and Bob reuse the same secret exponents across sessions, a future key compromise decrypts all past traffic. Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE/ECDHE — the E is the point) generates fresh exponents per session and discards them, so each session's key dies with the session. This is why modern TLS uses ephemeral key exchange: it is the difference between 'one breach exposes everything ever sent' and 'one breach exposes nothing already sent.' When you configure TLS, the setting you are actually choosing is whether past traffic survives future compromise. Choose ephemeral.
notes.title: Diffie-Hellman key exchange with small numbers

notes.body:
You now own the mechanism; here's what changes between the classroom and production — stated qualitatively, because the principle transfers and the parameters evolve. Size: your RSA used 12-bit n; real deployments use primes hundreds of digits long, making n thousands of bits. The number theory is byte-identical — Euclid, Euler, square-and-multiply — but the factoring problem at that scale is infeasible, which is the only thing standing between the eavesdropper and d. Padding: textbook RSA (what you just did) is deterministic — the same m always gives the same c — and malleable. Real RSA uses padding schemes that randomize encryption and add structure, defeating chosen-ciphertext attacks that textbook RSA falls to. Never deploy textbook RSA; know that it exists so you recognize it as a vulnerability when you see it. Key management dwarfs key math: the hardest part of real crypto is not the modular exponentiation — it is generating true randomness, storing private keys (HSMs, TPMs, vaults), rotating them, revoking compromised ones (CRLs, OCSP), and binding public keys to identities (certificates, certificate transparency). Most 'crypto failures' are key-management failures wearing a math costume. Quantum note, honestly framed: Shor's algorithm factors efficiently on a large enough quantum computer, which would break RSA and Diffie-Hellman as used today — this is why post-quantum migration is underway across the industry. You don't need the details today; you need the awareness that algorithm agility (the ability to swap algorithms) is a design requirement, not a luxury. Operational checklist for the security operator: know which of your systems rely on RSA/DH (TLS certificates, SSH host keys, VPNs, code signing); know their key sizes and expiry/rotation story; verify certificates actually chain to trusted roots rather than assuming; and when a vendor says 'military-grade encryption,' ask which algorithm, which key size, which padding, and who manages the keys — the four questions that separate engineering from marketing. Common mistake: believing crypto is 'set and forget.' Keys expire, algorithms weaken, implementations have bugs — cryptography is a maintenance discipline, and the math you learned is the foundation that lets you evaluate the maintenance.

Make this concrete with the inventory you should build this month: list every system that does public-key crypto — TLS certificates (with expiry dates and issuing CAs), SSH host keys (algorithm and size), VPN configurations (key exchange and authentication method), code-signing keys (who holds the private key, where), and backup encryption keys (where the keys live, who can recover them). For each, record algorithm, key size, expiry and rotation story, and private-key storage. You will find surprises — the cert expiring next month, the SSH host key generated in 2015, the backup encrypted with a key nobody can locate. Each surprise is a finding with a remediation date. Then set the maintenance cadence: certificate expiry monitoring with alerts at 30, 7, and 1 days; annual key-size policy review (the 'is 2048 still fine' question gets re-asked, not re-assumed); and a tested restore-from-backup that actually exercises the backup keys. Cryptography fails most often not in the math but in the maintenance — expired certs cause more outages than factored moduli. The operator who owns the inventory owns the crypto posture; the one who does not is hoping.
notes.title: From toy numbers to production: what actually changes

Compute fluently in modular arithmetic, including square-and-multiply exponentiation.
Generate an RSA keypair, encrypt and decrypt end-to-end with small primes, and prove correctness with Euler's theorem.
Execute a Diffie-Hellman exchange end-to-end and name the eavesdropper's view.
Distinguish textbook crypto from production crypto: sizes, padding, key management, algorithm agility.

quiz.explain: Extended Euclid gives 2×3120−367×17=1, so −367≡2753 is the inverse. Verify: 17×2753=46801=15×3120+1.

quiz.q: For RSA with p=61, q=53: φ(n) = ?

quiz.explain: 2790^2753 mod 3233=65 — the round trip closes because ed=46801=15×3120+1.

choices: (m^e)^d = m^(ed), and ed≡1 (mod φ(n)) so Euler's theorem reduces it to m
Because encryption and decryption use different moduli
It doesn't; RSA needs a trusted third party
quiz.explain: ed=15φ(n)+1, so m^(ed)=(m^φ)^15·m≡m. Euler's theorem is the correctness proof.
quiz.q: Why does RSA decryption recover the message?

quiz.explain: A=5^6 mod 23=8; B=5^15 mod 23=19. Verified by square-and-multiply.
quiz.q: DH with p=23, g=5, a=6, b=15: public values?

quiz.explain: Both sides compute g^(ab) mod p=2; the eavesdropper sees p, g, A, B but not the secret.
quiz.q: The DH shared secret in the worked example?

quiz.explain: Given g, p, g^a mod p, finding a is hard for large p — DH's security assumption.

choices: The math is identical but the numbers are toy-sized; production needs much larger primes, padding, and key management
Small primes make RSA faster and therefore better

quiz.explain: Mechanism ✓, sizes ✗. Never deploy textbook RSA: no padding, enumerable keyspace.

summary: The number theory under public-key cryptography: divisibility and primes, Euclid's algorithm worked by hand, extended Euclid for modular inverses, modular arithmetic, Euler's theorem, RSA key generation/encryption/decryption end-to-end with verified small-prime numbers, Diffie-Hellman worked both ways, and what changes in production.
